title: 128k-long-context-performance-deep-dive-acme-analytics
summary: Deep dive on running 128k+ context workloads. Covered attention/architecture optimizations, KV cache behavior, chunking strategy for retrieval augmented generation, batching and latency tradeoffs, quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run a 128k benchmark with Acme dataset, share kernel-level perf logs, and follow up with a pilot proposal and pricing.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-16
Time: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kumar (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (CTO, Acme), Sasha Lee (ML Eng, Acme), Marta Ruiz (Infra, Acme), Tom (Procurement, Acme)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda: run through our long-context runtime approach for 128k+, dig into KV cache behaviour, batching/latency, quantization, and VPC/on-prem notes. Priya will lead the perf bits.
[00:22] Daniel Park: Thanks Alex. We're really focused on two things: latency SLOs for interactive search over long docs and throughput/cost when running batched analytics jobs. We want to understand tradeoffs.
[00:38] Priya Kumar: Great. high-level first: to hit 128k+ we usually combine two pieces — sparse/local attention kernels + chunking w/ smart retrieval + KV-prefix caching. The runtime can keep KV cache hot for active prefixes to avoid recomputing keys/vals for repeated contexts.
[01:05] Sasha Lee: when you say "keep KV cache hot" — how much memory does that typically take per request? Our infra team is concerned about GPU memory on dedicated nodes.
[01:18] Priya Kumar: Good question. It depends on seq len and model size. For a 13B model at 128k tokens the KV memory is significant — roughly linear with sequence length. We maintain a working window and evict cold prefixes. In our Dedicated offering we use sharded KV across GPUs; for private you can increase local NVMe-backed spill. Note: transcription might hit "K V cash" in some auto-exports — that's just a transcription quirk.
[01:45] Marta Ruiz: NVMe spill sounds interesting. Is there a performance cliff when you spill to NVMe vs memory?
[01:53] Priya Kumar: Yes, there's a latency bump. We try to avoid mid-request spill by prefetching. For tail-heavy workloads we recommend increasing reserved RAM and using models with optimized attention. Also there's a big difference if you use 4-bit quant vs 8-bit — model activation memory goes down but you might lose a bit on exact token-level quality for QA tasks.
[02:20] Daniel Park: Could you talk a bit about attention optimizations? We saw papers about rotary + sparse attention. Which do you use?
[02:30] Priya Kumar: We support multiple kernels. For long context we use a combination: chunked attention that applies full attention within a local window and sparse global attention for retrieved chunks. We also implement caching-friendly attention kernels that avoid re-encoding earlier tokens when possible. For very long generative chains we sometimes fall back to an attention approximation that trades a small quality delta for 2-3x perf.
[02:58] Sasha Lee: any numbers — latency/throughput for a 128k forward pass? ballpark per token?
[03:06] Priya Kumar: Ballpark numbers vary a lot by model and hw. On a multi-GPU dedicated pool (A100-class) with local KV sharding we see ~15-40ms per 1k tokens for generation with optimized kernels. For single-request interactive SLOs we focus on prefix caching to reduce cold-starts to single-digit seconds; warm requests can be sub-second depending on output length. There's a lot of variance; we'll share concrete kernel traces.
[03:40] Alex Chen: I'll add that those numbers assume continuous batching and that batch size can increase effective throughput but will add to tail latency.
[03:52] Tom (Procurement): From a contract perspective we need SLA targets for latency and predictable cost. How deterministic are these numbers?
[04:02] Alex Chen: For Dedicated we can guarantee throughput curves under commit levels. For Hosted there is some variability but we provide percentiles. We'll include p50/p95/p99 in the runbook.
[04:18] Sasha Lee: Let's talk chunking strategies — we do RAG over corpora where individual docs are ~50-200k. How do you choose chunk size and overlap?
[04:32] Priya Kumar: We generally choose chunk sizes around 2k-8k tokens with 10-20% overlap for retrieval windows, but for 128k context we chunk more aggressively and maintain an LRU cache of high-similarity chunks in KV. Overlap is a trade: more overlap increases recall for windowed attention but increases KV memory and compute. We'll provide a heuristic script in the benchmark.
[04:58] Daniel Park: Does the Redwood runtime do chunking automatically or do you expect us to preprocess?
[05:06] Priya Kumar: Both. For Hosted/Dedicated we provide a chunking helper in SDK. You can also preprocess on your side. For private on-prem deployments teams often prefer to control chunking to match their retrieval layer.
[05:21] Sasha Lee: What about embeddings and indexing? We currently use FAISS with IVF+PQ. Does Redwood integrate with that or do you recommend your own vector store?
[05:32] Priya Kumar: We integrate with popular stores; many customers use FAISS. Our retrieval + chunking guide has recommended IVF settings for high-dimension vectors with long-doc retrieval. We'll share the doc.
[05:45] [06:00] Alex Chen: Quick note — we've got an internal bench spreadsheet that maps model/quant/profile to throughput. I'll share the link after the call.
[06:12] Marta Ruiz: Quantization — you mentioned 4-bit vs 8-bit. For our legal QA pipeline we need near lossless accuracy. Do you have metrics on hallucination/regression after quant?
[06:25] Priya Kumar: We run eval suites tied to your prompts. 4-bit (QLoRA-style) is good for many workloads but can change token probabilities; for high-stakes QA we usually recommend 8-bit or mixed precision and run an eval set to ensure no regression. Redwood Optimize can simulate and recommend quant profiles per workload. Expect a small drop in F1/EM for some tasks; we'll capture that in the benchmark.
[06:58] Sasha Lee: How do you handle batching — for our interactive API we want low tail latency but for nightly jobs we want max throughput. Can the same cluster do both?
[07:12] Priya Kumar: Yes if you partition capacity. Our Dedicated offering allows reserved pools for low-latency paths and separate batch nodes. Smart routing will send requests by policy. For private deployments you can run multiple instance types and our runtime will route accordingly. Batching windows and max_wait settings should be tuned: shorter waits keep latency low but reduce GPU utilization.
[07:40] Daniel Park: Any difference in behavior when running in a VPC vs Redwood-hosted?
[07:47] Priya Kumar: In VPC/private you control networking and can avoid egress costs; however telemetry and control plane integration is different. We ship a private control plane that connects to your KMS and audit logs. Performance-wise the runtime is the same, but provisioning and autoscaling might be constrained by your infra quotas. Also note we offer an on-prem package for fully air-gapped setups but that adds ops work.
[08:12] Sasha Lee: Security: does the KV or cached prefixes persist on disk? We're subject to retention rules.
[08:20] Priya Kumar: We expose retention controls. For Hosted we keep ephemeral caches and can configure TTLs and purge policies; for Dedicated/Private you can enforce disk encryption and custom retention via KMS/HSM. We'll send SOC2 and encryption docs.
[08:38] [09:00] Alex Chen: Let's go into a mini-case study — a customer did a 100k -> 128k migration and saw a 2.8x cost increase without KV sharding. Priya, can you explain?
[09:12] Priya Kumar: Sure. Cost grows roughly with tokens processed and with increased kernel complexity. Without shardable KV the memory pressure forced smaller batch sizes and more cross-GPU communication, which increases time per token. Sharding KV and using optimized kernels reduced RPCs and kernel launches. We'll include kernel flamegraphs in the logs.
[09:42] Sasha Lee: Are there any open-source kernel projects you build on? I'm trying to map to our infra team's existing work.
[09:50] Priya Kumar: We upstream some kernels and also maintain proprietary optimizations. The kernels align with Triton-style approaches and leverage custom fused attention kernels when available. There may be name mismatches in the transcript — sometimes "Triton" becomes "try-ton" in auto text.
[10:08] Daniel Park: For our pilot can you outline the benchmark plan?
[10:16] Priya Kumar: Yes — step 1: you give us sample corpus + typical query set; step 2: we run cold/warm benchmarks across profiles (float16, 8-bit, 4-bit) capturing p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, KB per token, and memory spikes; step 3: we iterate on chunking and caching heuristics; step 4: produce a recommendation and pilot config. We'll need 48-72 hours to run a first sweep.
[10:44] Sasha Lee: What about cost modeling — can you estimate $/million tokens for each profile?
[10:51] Alex Chen: We'll provide a cost model based on your projected workload and the benchmark results. For Dedicated we can give committed pricing.
[11:02] Tom (Procurement): Any blockers for a pilot — legal or infra?
[11:08] Alex Chen: We need an MSA and an NDA (if not already). For private/on-prem there are additional on-site validation steps. For Hosted or Dedicated pilot it's straightforward.
[11:18] Daniel Park: Ok let's recap next steps.
[11:22] Alex Chen: Recap: Alex to send runbook, kernel logs, and bench template; Priya to draft pilot config; Sasha to send sample docs and query sets; we'll aim to kick off week of 2026-04-27.
[11:38] Sasha Lee: One last micro question — do you recommend chunking by semantic boundaries or fixed token counts for legal docs?
[11:46] Priya Kumar: Semantic boundaries are better for recall and reduce split-entity issues, but they're harder to compute at scale. For legal docs we usually do a hybrid: semantic first pass, then fixed token windowing for the long tail.
[11:58] Daniel Park: Great, thanks everyone.
[12:05] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts. Link: Benchmark spreadsheet (private): https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/acme-128k (shared after call).

End of transcript.
